items.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Growth and Sustainability of Ed-Tech Start-ups in Uttar Pradesh
items.abstract: The education technology (Ed-Tech) industry is evolving rapidly thanks to the power of Artificial Intelligence (AI), which is now being used to personalize learning, automate evaluation, create intelligent content and manage student data and information, as well as streamline business operations. The rise of skills and technologies like AI is transforming the landscape of Ed-Tech startups in Uttar Pradesh by enhancing their competitive edge, reducing operational expenses, boosting user engagement, and optimizing educational delivery. This study focuses on the importance and contribution of Artificial Intelligence in the development and sustainability of the start-ups in the Ed-Tech sector in Uttar Pradesh. It emphasizes the ways in which AI aids companies in growing, enhancing their operations, innovating, pleasing customers, customizing learning, and staying sustainable over time. The study also reveals key challenges in the implementation of AI such as cost of implementation, lack of skilled expertise, privacy issues, technology constraints, and change resistance. Descriptive research design is proposed with the help of primary data collection from selected Ed-Tech start-ups and their employees/manager in UP. The analysis is based on percentages, looking at trends in AI use and impact on business performance and sustainability. The results of the study will benefit entrepreneurs, Ed-Tech managers, policy makers and others as they look for ways to implement AI effectively. The results could help in understanding the role of AI in promoting sustainable growth of the nascent Ed-Tech ecosystem in UP, if used responsibly and strategically

items.title: Socio-technical co-adaptation: Digital integration and workplace learning
items.abstract: This article examines the socio-technical dynamics of introducing the TEMA decision support application into a high-reliability organisation (HRO), addressing the research gap that often overlooks the relationship between new technology and established practices. A qualitative, interpretive case study was conducted within a rescue department, involving 11 officers. Data were triangulated through pre-simulation trainer debriefings, in-situ simulation observations, and post-simulation debriefings. Vignettes were used as micro-cases of lived experiences, and to strengthen ecological validity and interpretive depth. The study reveals friction points in joint optimisation due to technical usability, language incongruency, and perceived trust in artificial intelligence (AI) generated outputs. The findings are integrated into the Socio-Technical Co-adaptation Spiral, a model conceptualising technical friction as a concrete experience that can initiate a cycle of reflection, sense-making and adaptation. The Spiral contributes to OL and STS theory by showing how socio-technical friction can create conditions for double-loop learning within an HRO.

items.title: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
items.abstract: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.

items.title: Super Intelligence in Healthcare: A Systematic Review of Systemic Risks, Ethical Dilemmas, and Governance Frameworks
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from narrow, task-specific tools toward general-purpose systems whose capabilities may eventually exceed expert human performance across most cognitive tasks. Healthcare is among the most consequential domains in which such systems will be deployed, yet governance arrangements remain calibrated to narrow software rather than to open-ended, self-improving agents. Objective: To synthesise evidence on the systemic risks, ethical dilemmas, and governance frameworks relevant to advanced and prospectively superintelligent AI in healthcare, and to expose the gap between promotional claims and the empirical record. Methods: A PRISMA 2020-guided structured synthesis was conducted in two streams: (A) a defined corpus of 117 bibliographic records, screened against explicit eligibility criteria, and (B) 51 purposively selected benchmark sources providing comparative empirical, ethical, and regulatory evidence. Findings were organised through thematic synthesis and critical appraisal, and compared across regulatory regimes. Results: Of the 117 corpus records, 72 were excluded at title screening, 45 were retained, and 33 formed the core synthesis. Four convergent findings emerged. First, the evidence for clinical benefit is dominated by retrospective, single-site, and narrowly benchmarked studies. Second, systemic risks (automation bias, deskilling, correlated failure, security vulnerability, and concentration of power) scale non-linearly with capability. Third, principle-based ethics frameworks are widely endorsed but weakly operational. Fourth, existing regulatory regimes address device performance but not alignment, accountability for autonomous action, or catastrophic tail risk. Conclusion: Governance of superintelligent healthcare AI cannot be deferred until such systems exist. A staged, evidence-gated framework that couples capability thresholds to oversight obligations, liability allocation, and equity safeguards is proposed.
